speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. C-190, to amend the Bank of Canada Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DIRECTION OF MONETARY POLICY, CASH RESERVES, ETC.
speechtext: Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DIRECTION OF MONETARY POLICY, CASH RESERVES, ETC.
speechtext:
A bill to revise the Bank of Canada Act was introduced at the last session. It received second reading and was referred to committee but lapsed with the ending of the session on June 30. The present bill is identical with that introduced a year ago except for one minor addition.
The principal change in the Bank , of Canada statute which is being proposed is for the purpose of clarifying the relationship between the government and the central bank by authorizing the government, under conditions which are specified in the bill, to give the bank a directive concerning monetary policy.
Another important change is to authorize the bank to impose and vary a minimum secondary reserve requirement for the chartered banks in place of its present power to vary their minimum cash reserve requirement. A number of technical changes are also being proposed and some revisions to eliminate obsolete provisions of the act.

I rise on a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker. If I do so at this time, it is because of a statement

I made in this house on Wednesday, May 25, that is, last week. I must apologize at once to the house if my remarks created some confusion or were misinterpreted. I never intended that my remarks should be interpreted as they were. First of all, it was never my intention to involve or connect the suicides in the Guadeloupe area with the winter works program and even less with the municipal council of the parish. Also, when I mentioned that those suicides had been committed, I had in mind localities surrounding Notre-Dame-de-la-Guadeloupe, because I asked the future minister of manpower (Mr. Marchand) to conduct an investigation in the case of parishes surrounding Notre-Dame-de-la-Guadeloupe.
It is unfortunate that this happened, but if it turned out that way, it is because I said the R.C.M.P. could inquire into the matter of winter works, since charges of fraud have been made, and that such offences come under the Criminal Code. I also referred to the matter of suicides, because I felt the R.C.M.P. might conduct an investigation in that connection.
I apologize for not having made the difference, for there is no relationship between winter works and those suicides. I had mentioned seven suicides by hanging and now Le Devoir sought information from the local coroner and there may have been at least a dozen, in the past six years, as mentioned in Le Devoir.
It is then not a question of suicides. I wanted to mark the difference and to enlighten the house on this question because I never intended to relate such suicides to the question of winter works. speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: QUEBEC LONGSHOREMEN'S STRIKE-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would ask the Minister of Labour to give us a report on the abortive proceedings regarding settlement of the longshoremen's strike, and after he has given his report I hope to ask him some supplementary questions.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. R. Nicholson (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: QUEBEC LONGSHOREMEN'S STRIKE-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope you will pardon me if my answer is a little longer than it normally would be to a question on orders of the day.
Together with two of my colleagues, the Minister of Industry and the President of the Privy Council, as well as Judge Rene Lippe, the government appointed mediator, my deputy minister and other senior officials, I met here in Ottawa with representatives of the two parties to the dispute on the evening of Friday last. I might say that the meeting lasted several hours and the discussions were both informative and useful.
The Minister of Industry and I met again with these groups on Sunday afternoon and evening in Montreal. I might say that the longshoremen's association had made certain

May 30, 1966

proposals late in the week which were considered by the shipping federation over the week end. The federation indicated that they were prepared, inter alia, to agree to a very substantial increase in pay in order to bring about a settlement; but they stressed, I think quite properly, the desirability of higher productivity during the second year of the proposed agreement.
In the course of the meetings I made some suggestions which were discussed at length. Unfortunately no solution was reached.
While the discussions terminated without a solution after many hours of earnest and frank debate, there were some important accomplishments, and at least the differences between the parties with reference to wages and fringe benefits were narrowed. I believe that with further serious discussion and, if necessary, further mediation a solution will be found within a reasonable time. Judge Lippe is closely following the situation, as I am, and our good offices-that is the way the parties described them last night-are available to both parties at any time if requested.
Mr. Speaker, as I said in the house on Friday last I believe that in most industrial disputes the natural process of collective bargaining brings about the best and most effective solution. In spite of the seriousness of the present situation I remain convinced that with a sincere desire on the part of both parties to bring about a solution, the remaining differences will be resolved within a reasonable time.

subtopic: QUEBEC LONGSHOREMEN'S STRIKE-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would now ask the minister what he means by a reasonable time, because this has been the explanation all along as they have dillied and dallied. subtopic: QUEBEC LONGSHOREMEN'S STRIKE-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext: Well, Mr. Speaker, I think the answer to that is very simple. Nearly 3,000 of the workers involved live and work in Montreal and I had two of my colleagues from Montreal with me.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question. subtopic: QUEBEC LONGSHOREMEN'S STRIKE-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that is hardly an accurate summary of the situation. There is more than one point still outstanding, though admittedly the question of productivity during the second year of the contract is an important one. As I have said, very substantial increases-some say fantastic increases, I would suggest-in pay were offered. In return for these, the shipping federation has suggested, and I think properly, that they might expect increased productivity during the second year of the agreement.
Perhaps I should say at this point that one of the suggestions that I made, which seemed to have been received favourably by both sides, was in inquiry into working conditions in the three St. Lawrence ports concerned, which would include an objective look into the matter of increased productivity and not only the structure and size of the work gangs but also the use of new equipment and other items of that nature. This was accepted in principle by both sides, and it was generally agreed that if such a commission were set up that they would look into all aspects of working conditions. A second substantial increase would take place with the implementation of any recommendation which might come out of this.
In fact, if no recommendations were to come out of it there still would be a further increase; but in connection with the proposal for reorganization of the gangs, the suggestion was made that there might be some lay-offs involved. The shipping federation offers job security for all the people who had worked for more than a given period of last year; in fact they offered job security for all those who had worked, I think, for more than 15 or 16 weeks. That was put forward for consideration. This is where the figure of 85 per cent comes in. I am advised that the other 15 per cent or less comprises the casual groups, such as the taxi drivers, students and those who work for a limited period each year.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a word or two in support of the amendment before the question is put. My position was made clear on the discussion of the estimates of the Department of Justice for the year 1965-66, which were debated earlier this session. I took the opportunity at that time to refer to the proposal to divide the duties formerly discharged by the Minister of Justice between three departments.
My view then expressed was that instead of this division, which I believe will increase the difficulties of co-operation and co-ordination between the various branches and services that now report to the Minister of Justice, co-operation and co-ordination which are vital and are becoming more vital, the
May 30, 1966	COMMONS
reorganizing and strengthening of these functions would best be served by maintaining one ministry and Department of Justice but providing for three deputy ministers, with three divisions or main branches in that department. There would be a deputy minister in charge of over-all administration who would be directly responsible for the present functions of the department, giving legal advice to the government, the drafting of legislation and those functions which might be termed strictly the departmental functions of the present Department of Justice.
Second, there would be a deputy minister in charge of a division of enforcement which would include the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, the combines investigation branch and the bankruptcy division.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
Third, it would include a deputy minister in charge of corrections, including the penitentiaries branch, the parole services and the functions related to the correctional program.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW DEPARTMENTS
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question? Do I understand his suggestion to be that there ought to be three deputy ministers, in other words, that there should be, in addition to the present deputy minister and an associate deputy minister, one more deputy minister?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW DEPARTMENTS
speechtext:
My suggestion is that there ought to be three deputies, one to be known as the deputy minister of justice, the other to be known as the deputy minister of enforcements and the third to be known as the deputy minister of corrections, all reporting to the one minister of justice. The deputy minister of justice would be responsible under the minister for co-ordination of the three divisions, with the minister, however, having responsibility in cabinet and a concomitant responsibility therefore to parliament and to the country for the co-ordination and effective discharge of all the services and duties of the Department of Justice.
In my view this would be a far more effective way of ensuring co-ordination than the present proposal. I agree with the solicitor general that the duties of the Minister of Justice have increased. This is inevitable with the growth of the country. But in my view the way to assist him better to discharge the increase in responsibilities would be by a reorganization along the lines I have suggested.
I must say that, to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Greenwood on
DEBATES	5685
Government Organization Wednesday dealing with this proposal the Solicitor General made a reply which, while I accept the logic in it, in my humble submission did not take account of the facts. I assure the minister that I do not wish to be in any sense improperly derogatory about the argument he has used. But it does seem to me that it is an argument which is attractive in theory more than it is sound in fact, in the light of the realities of the situation. There is enough difficulty now in ensuring co-operation and co-ordination.
In his reply the minister based his position in part upon the experience in the United Kingdom. Although I am very much impressed with the desirability of studying the precedents and examples set by the oldest existing parliamentary democracy in the world, I respectfully suggest that the position in the United Kingdom is not in this case as valid a precedent for us to follow as in some others, because of the peculiar problems which, in the field of the administration of justice and enforcement of law, are created by the differences in governmental jurisdiction in Canada, because of our division into a federal and ten provincial governments, a situation not paralleled in any respect in the United Kingdom.
The particular situation in Canada involves constant problems of co-operation and consultation with provincial governments and the very frequent consultations between the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada with provincial Attorneys General not only with respect to constitutional matters but with respect to legal matters and those having to do with law enforcement generally. We are entering a period when the problem of combating organized crime in this country is assuming ever more serious proportions and involving ever more serious responsibilities of government. A special responsibility is imposed on the federal government by reason of the fact that since there are people who are prepared to organize crime on a national basis it surely follows that the fighting of this trend should be nationally co-ordinated.
Indeed, it seems to me that many measures ought to be initiated by the central government on behalf of the people of Canada generally in order that our program to counter organized crime is as effective as the program of those who organize crime on a national scale. This must involve increasing consultation and co-ordination with provincial Attorneys General and law enforcement
5686	COMMONS
Government Organization agencies, and also involves the constitutional aspect.
It seems to me, however, that by the step taken here, we are inevitably creating a multiplicity of channels of communication and increasing the difficulties of co-ordination and co-operation, whereas if there were one minister of justice responsible for the co-ordination of all these functions many difficulties would be avoided.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, I want to say a word about the situation respecting the R.C.M.P. In what I have said before and in what I am about to say, the solicitor general knows that I make no reflections upon him personally. I express the hope, if the government goes ahead with the setting up of this department, which I am opposed to, that the minister will be able to ensure that the prestige and function of the force are maintained at the highest level.
But I doubt very much that the Department of the Solicitor General can or should achieve the standing and prestige of a properly constituted and administered Department of Justice, which in my view, by the very nature of its primary function, is one of the most important departments of government. It is the department responsible for advising the government generally and for ensuring that all actions of the government conform to the law and are of the proper standard. It is the department responsible for ensuring that government actions are in accordance with constitutional responsibility and authority. All these functions plus many others which have traditionally been discharged by the department and its minister over the years have by their very nature ensured the seniority of this department, not because of the persons involved in it but because of the function of the department and its head.
For this reason I think it is an undesirable development for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, which has traditionally been responsible to the Minister of Justice, to be taken out of or removed from a relationship with that department. I feel that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police has not been well served in recent years by certain developments, the details of which I do not propose to go into at this time. Through no fault of its own the prestige of the force has suffered. I think it is incumbent upon the government to take every step to ensure that the prestige of the force, which remains ready and able to discharge its responsibilities and to live up to its standards and prestige, is restored and not diminished.

DEBATES	May 30, 1966
At another and more appropriate time I propose to discuss specific proposals by which that can be done. I am talking now only about the proposition of removing the force from the Department of Justice and placing it under the proposed Department of the Solicitor General. This, I think, is again a move against the trend which I think should be followed, the trend of supporting, reinforcing and re-elevating, if you like, the prestige and stature of Canada's central law enforcement body.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
It will therefore be seen, Mr. Chairman, that while the amendment itself does not go far enough it should nevertheless have the effect of preserving the relationship between the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, the Department of Justice and Minister of Justice. To the extent, therefore, that it removes one aspect of the proposed division I support the amendment although, speaking for myself and for the members of this party, whether or not the amendment carriers we shall oppose the clause which gives effect to the other division of the functions of the Minister of Justice.
Amendment (Mr. Brewin) negatived: Yeas, 42; nays, 66.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW DEPARTMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this bill is, of course an attempt to reassess the functions of government and to devise government machinery capable of handling those functions. Since the beginning of this debate it has been clear to at least some members of the government that these reassessments and changes are not necessarily final. The Prime Minister himself, in his introductory remarks strongly indicated that the machinery of government will be changing continually because of the needs of the times in which we live.
We in this party believe there is one change which should be made without delay. Both in this chamber and in various parts of Canada outside this house, attention has been called to the need to establish a department of government to protect the affairs of consumers. A former minister of the crown, speaking in Toronto, pointed out the need
May 30, 1966	COMMONS
which he saw arising in the near future for the establishment of three departments, one of which would be a department of consumer affairs.
I see no reason why the government should hesitate to proceed along these lines while this legislation is in progress. Demands for such a department are being made continuously in all parts of the country and will become increasingly heavy. I suggest, therefore, that it would be wise to make the change now without waiting even for another year, by which time the demand will be even greater than it is today.
In an attempt to avoid a solution which would mean the setting up of an entirely new department and involve large expenditures of money and so on, alternative suggestions have been made. I believe we have found a solution which is workable and which would be acceptable to the government. Indeed, this approach was opened up by the Prime Minister himself speaking in this debate the other day. The proposal I have in mind is nothing more or less than the utilization of an existing department which could be called the department of consumer affairs and which would gather together all the work in this field now being done by many government departments.
I should like to read from the speech which the Prime Minister made on May 24 in the course of this debate, as reported at page 5430 of Hansard. I believe his words in this connection were significant and very much to the point. He said:
One of the matters which will have to be considered early in the establishment of the department of the registrar general is to what extent it can further assist and protect the Canadian consumer, which is a matter that was mentioned in the discussion on the resolution, especially by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Mae-Innis). The Department of Trade and Commerce, the Department of National Health and Welfare, and the Department of Agriculture-
The right hon. gentleman might have mentioned several other departments as well:
-now have active consumer protection roles within their own departmental areas of responsibility, but there may be other areas in which the federal government can develop consumer protection programs and there may be a real need to co-ordinate what is being done now in a number of departments.
It is the government's intention to ask the Economic Council to look at the field of consumer affairs, along with some of the other functions now to be undertaken by the registrar general under the legislation before us, with a view to providing advice as to the courses of action that seem best
DEBATES	5687
Government Organization
suited to meeting the needs of the Canadian people and the Canadian economy in the consumer field.
I have no doubt that the Prime Minister and the other members of his government are fully aware of the need for a department of consumer affairs. We can understand their reluctance to create a new department with all that would be entailed in the recruitment of staff and so on. But we echo the words of the Prime Minister himself in this regard. There is already in contemplation the setting up of a department which would have a large measure of responsibility for consumer affairs-the department of the registrar general. It is to this department that we wish to direct our amendment this afternoon.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)

In our party, we are quite used to making the ammunition and seeing the others use it.
The main thing is that the well-being of our consumers be protected as effectively as possible and with the least possible delay.
Therefore, seconded by the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Saltsman), I propose the following amendment:
That Bill C-178 be amended by changing the heading preceding clause 6 from "Department of the Registrar General" to "Department of Consumer Affairs", and that clause 6 be amended by changing the words "Department of the Registrar General" to the words "Department of Consumer Affairs", and also by changing the words "Registrar General of Canada" to the words "Minister of Consumer Affairs", wherever the said words appear in subclause (1) and subclause (2) of the said clause 6.

Mr. Chairman, I have copies of the amendment in both French and English.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW DEPARTMENTS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, following the remarks of the member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis)-in her case, I should say Vancouver-Queensway-and the amendment she moved-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW DEPARTMENTS
speechtext: That is good.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW DEPARTMENTS
speechtext:
-and the statements or suggestions made concerning the nature of the department, I should like to say a few words about the new proposed department, that of the registrar general of Canada. I shall attempt to prove that the meaning of the title proposed in the amendment is too restricted in relation to the duties the department will be called upon to perform, but that, on the other hand, what should be determined is
5688	COMMONS
Government Organization precisely the essential and actual nature of the powers devolved to the new minister. I feel that after studying the wording of the proposed legislation, as well as the powers suggested for the Registrar General, everybody will be satisfied that such powers include, in addition to others, those designed to protect the interests of consumers.

The new department of the registrar general groups together a number of agencies whose primary responsibilities can be described as reflecting public policy toward business organization. The principal agencies are the office of the Director of Investigation and Research under the Combines Investigation Act and the related Restrictive Trades Practices Commission, the office of the Commissioner of Patents, having jurisdiction over patents and copyrights, the office of the Registrar of Trademarks, the office of the Superintendent of Bankruptcy and the corporations branch.
All of these agencies have been engaged in the administration of the ground rules established by parliament for the conduct of those engaged in business under our free enterprise economy.
Each of the laws has developed over the years, starting with fairly primitive controls to prevent frauds and other flagrant abuses. The various bodies of law, such as the anticombines law and patents law, tended to develop independently of each other, to be the object of separate disciplines, and to be administered by different government departments. As our economy became more advanced and more complicated, corporations took on and continue to take on a greater importance in relation to the national economic objectives. It is essential that the legislation which provides the ground rules within which corporations must operate is designed and co-ordinated in such a way as to encourage maximum efficiency and responsiveness to the needs of the public at large.

These laws provide the basic framework for corporate activity and as such they are laws of general application. They are readily distinguished from legislation which arises out of economic policies designed to improve the performance of particular industries or to influence particular activities in the economy. They are, nevertheless, an integral part of the economic fabric of the country and it is important to recognize that each agency is

DEBATES	May 30, 1966
affected by and affects economic policy in other areas.
As these are laws of general application, their economic impact ordinarily becomes apparent only in the long run; but they are no less important for this reason than economic policies which have a more immediate impact upon the economy.
There are a number of important reasons for grouping these agencies in the new department. Each agency shares the same ultimate goal of encouraging the corporate sector of the economy to work more smoothly and efficiently while remaining consistent with the public interest. Each agency is linked in a direct and special way with at least one of the others. The work Of each agency is based on detailed statutes and a large body of case law. For this reason the agencies are administered to a large extent by lawyers. There is a danger that, in isolation, the legislation may be administered and revised with a purely technical bias rather than in terms of its fundamental social and economic purposes.
The Combines Investigation Act is based on the principle that under normal circumstances competition provides the greatest spur to efficiency and to the best allocation of economic resources in the private sector of the economy. This is sometimes forgotten in the more immediate concern about possible exploitation of consumers or about the inequitable treatment of some economic units by others. Where competition is effective, efficiency is rewarded and inefficiency is penalized. In the long run, efficient corporations grow and inefficient ones decline. Scarce resources are therefore channelled into the hands of those who use them best.
Combines policy is closely linked with other government economic policy. For example, it is evident that if economies of large scale in a particular industry are such that the Canadian market cannot sustain enough producers to provide effective competition, appropriate tariff policy may make it possible to solve the problem by encouraging concentration while at the same time expanding competition from foreign companies. This would transfer to the public some of the gains in efficiency arising out of the consolidation of the industry into a few large corporate units. [DOT] (4:10 p.m.)

Although legal proceedings are necessarily important in the administration of the Combines Investigation Act, the objectives sought by the legislation are economic. For
May 30, 1966

these reasons it is most desirable that the Combines Investigation Act be administered in a department more directly concerned with economic policy. The Canada Corporation Act, in conjunction with its provincial counterparts, provides the basic framework on which modern corporations are constructed. Although the federal act recently has been amended the proposed Ontario legislation probably will be making still greater advances which most likely will require a review of the Canada Corporation Act to make sure not only that it is fully co-ordinated with the government's economic objectives but also that it keeps pace with legislative advances in this field.
Incidentally, the proposed Ontario legislation stresses the close relationship between corporate affairs of a continuing nature and those relating to the issue and sale of securities. Through adequate disclosure requirements and regulations of such matters as insiders' trading, this legislation in conjunction with similar provincial legislation can make an important contribution to the efficient allocation of resources in the economy. This will happen in a number of ways. Lack of information and unregulated insider transactions cause investors to mistrust company directors and officers. Potential investors are thus less likely to invest or their funds are unlikely to be well invested. Shareholders have great difficulty in forcing management to be efficient if they do not have access to well prepared and complete company accounts. The absence of information may lead to a failure to identify those sectors of the economy which are inefficient as a result of restrictive practices or lack of new competitors. A federal-provincial meeting of officials will be held on June 27 and 28 and will consider the whole field of financial disclosure and securities regulation. These are areas in which the federal government may assist and in this respect the registrar general's department will have its role to play.

The principal justification of the patent system is that it encourages research and development and thus contributes to the acceleration of economic progress. It will do this, however, only where it harmonizes with other economic policies. A patent is a temporary monopoly granted to the inventor by the state; and government policy on patents
Government Organization clearly must be co-ordinated with government policy on competition. The close connection between the two has been recognized in the past and there are references in the Combines Act to patent and trade mark abuses and in the Patent Act to restraint-of-trade abuses. In addition, the Trade Marks Act by its nature, is concerned with what is termed unfair competition such as when attempts are made to pass-off as the same, goods of a different origin.
The patent system should not be permitted to frustrate any benefits anticipated from a reduction in other obstacles to trade. Strong views have been expressed that as trade barriers are reduced, industrialists are likely to place greater emphasis on industrial property rights to replace the geographical protection lost by the reduction of tariff barriers. The patent system should not encourage the creation of an inefficient structure of Canadian industry by compelling the working of patents in Canada when it is otherwise uneconomic for production to take place. The Ilsley Commission on Patents devoted considerable attention to this particular matter. A very high percentage of all Canadian patents are owned by non-residents and there is danger where patents act as a barrier to the entry of new firms, that the patent system will increase unnecessarily foreign control of Canadian industry.

The new department will have to consider also the implications of the registered user provisions of the Trade Marks Act. These provisions are comparatively new and are a departure from the theory that a trade mark should identify a single origin. Problems may arise where other Canadian companies must compete against a registered user in Canada of an American trade mark because the registered user normally will benefit from overflow advertising from the United States. All of these matters have been or will be considered by an interdepartmental committee which has been studying the recommendations of the Royal Commission on Patents.
The smooth and efficient working of the economic system obviously is injured by the economic dislocation and waste which results from unnecessary bankruptcies. Perhaps more important, unnecessary bankruptcies tend to produce a general decline in investor confidence and a greater reluctance to take risks and to innovate. To the extent that
May 30, 1966

Government Organization adequate disclosure requirements and securities regulations are introduced in Canada, the number of needless or fraudulent bankruptcies may be reduced and the work of the bankruptcy branch made more effective. Close liaison between the bankruptcy branch and the corporations branch will make it possible for more effective action to be taken against those dishonest persons who hide behind corporate laws.
The role of the registrar general initially will be to administer existing statutes along these lines to ensure that they are well co-ordinated with each other and with the general aspects of government economic policy. The field of consumer protection has been the subject of a good deal of research in many jurisdictions and in some has given rise to new legislation. These developments are being followed with interest and may point to the possibility of fruitful action at the federal level in the interest of the consumer and the investing public. The importance which the house attaches to this problem has been reflected in the establishment of a special committee on the price of drugs, a joint Senate and House of Commons committee on consumer credit, and in many other expressions of opinion within parliament in recent years. At present there are, I think, 13 private members' bills or measures which concern either consumer credit or in some fashion the interests of the consumers.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
To the extent that there has been any tendency to create industry oriented departments without providing a corresponding organization to have particular responsibilities for the consumer and the public at large in corporate matters, the new department presents an immediate opportunity to correct this deficiency. The registrar general will have a voice in the development of the government's economic policy and he will have to see to it that as policy develops it is in harmony with the philosophy of the statutes for which he is responsible or that decisions are made to modify the statutes.

In other words, I believe it will be readily understood that the new department of the registrar general will, on the whole, be entrusted with co-ordinating, in the interest of the depositors as well as the consumers and any other party interested in either of those fields, such federal legislation concerns the
[Mr. Favreau.l
application of the major economic policies of the government.
In this sense, it can be understood that this department, although one of its functions will be to safeguard the rights and interest of the consumers, will have broader duties which will also comprise the application of the statutes to other areas.
For those reasons, I believe that limiting the title to that of department of consumer affairs would be unduly to restrict the scope of the jurisd ction of this new department. I think that the title of registrar general, which immediately gives the idea of registration and control as concerns federal affairs, is closer to the very character of the department than the name now suggested.
Be that as it may, for want of a name more closely adapted to the character of the functions proposed for the new department, I believe that what matters is to ascertain in depth the very functions of the new minister. On this score, I feel the title is much less significant than the substance and it would be proper for the house to maintain the suggested title of registrar general which is one of long standing in the traditions of government, one that has always been in existence and one which reflects adequately enough, at least an important part of the role of the one responsible for the new department.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the minister
has dealt with this matter as though we were considering clause 1 of a separate bill and I propose to deal with it in the same way. I have said before and I repeat that, like the hon. member for Kamloops, I believe the only method by which organized criminal activities in this country can be combatted at all is on an organized basis. For that reason it is heartening to note that bankruptcy legislation once again will come under the same umbrella of jurisdiction as companies and winding-up legislation because these things are inseparable. However, as I see it, there still exists a great gap in that the enforcement agency will come under a separate minister.
When organized rackets exist in more lucrative areas, namely, in respect of bankruptcies, surely the enforcement of federal legislation should come under the jurisdiction of the same minister who is responsible for the administration of that legislation in breach of which these frauds are perpetrated. As the hon. member for Kamloops has mentioned, there is a responsibility and indeed, an urgent
May 30, 1966

necessity for federal authorities to co-ordinate all activities in this regard. This has been suggested in respect of fraudulent bankruptcies and bankruptcy legislation under the jurisdiction of the new department.
I should like to refer to one specific aspect of this matter which has been raised by the press, in comments both inside and outside this house and by the Minister of Justice in correspondence he has had with me. This matter relates to fraudulent bankruptcies and the proper course, if I may condense it in that fashion, to be followed by individuals who are interested in seeing a discontinuance of fraudulent activities by any person.
On May 11, 1966, I received a letter from the Minister of Justice which I propose to read into the record in order to make sure that the facts are stated correctly. It is dated May 11, is under the letterhead of the Minister of Justice, and reads as follows:
Dear Mr. Nielsen:
A Canadian Press story in this morning's edition of the Globe and Mail states that you told reporters in Windsor, yesterday, that you had information on the involvement of federal officials in fraudulent bankruptcies.
I am writing to you as the minister responsible for matters relating to bankruptcy, and respectfully request that you provide me or the Royal Canadian Mounted Police with any information you have in support of these allegations.
I assure you that my department and the federal government is anxious to ensure that no federal officials shall be a party to any wrongdoing.
Yours very truly,
Lucien Cardin, Minister of Justice
I did not reply to that letter between that date and May 16, which was the date of a second letter directed to me by the Minister of Justice on his stationery. For some reason this one was registered. It stated:
Dear Mr. Nielsen:
A Canadian Press story in the May 11, 1966, edition of the Globe and Mail states that you told reporters in Windsor, last Tuesday, that you had information on the involvement of federal officials in fraudulent bankruptcies.
I am writing to you as the minister responsible for matters relating to bankruptcy, and respectfully request that you provide me or the Royal Canadian Mounted Police with any information you have in support of these allegations.
I assure you that my department and the federal government are anxious to ensure that no federal officials shall be a party to any wrongdoing.
Yours very truly,
Lucien Cardin,
Minister of Justice
In view of the fact that this matter has been raised by members of this house, the
Government Organization press and the minister I have had considerable difficulty and I have discussed my difficulty with the Solicitor General. It relates to the obligation of a member of parliament to this institution, the freedom of access of citizens to members and the information which comes to members as a result of that access accompanied by a request that it be kept confidential and that the names of these people not be disclosed.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
I am glad to see that the President of the Privy Council is paying attention to what I have to say at this time. I should like to deal with two other facets of this matter. The first relates to the knowledge which the Minister of Justice had or should have had before he wrote the two letters which I have read. He knows, for instance, that I disclosed of my own volition certain information which was of substantial assistance in the Banks case. He knows too that I had discussions with officers of the force with respect to fraudulent bankruptcies before he wrote me these letters. Since that time I have had further discussions at the request of the informant. Therein lies the important difference between the obligation that a member has of his own volition, the obligation that he owes to the citizen to maintain free access to his member and the obligation the member has with respect to the institution itself.
But, sir, I would suggest to the minister who will likely be the new registrar general that there are certain investigative procedures that should be followed, and followed now, in cases such as fraudulent bankruptcies. There is a chain of investigative processes that parliament has authorized the Minister of Justice to follow in an inquiry into bankruptcy matters under the minister's jurisdiction, and we will clothe the new registrar general with the same kind of authority because these matters are imminently to come under this minister's jurisdiction if he indeed is going to be the registrar general as I anticipate.
He should follow these procedures and not,
I suggest with respect and with no intention of innuendo or anything else with regard to the Minister of Justice, write members of parliament letters which in effect can be interpreted as "lettres de cachet", as I think they are referred to in French. When the minister wishes to investigate the conduct of any of the public matters with which he is charged by parliament the procedure for him
5692	COMMONS
Government Organization to follow is clearly laid out for him by parliament. This was one of the purposes of my asking the Prime Minister the question I did at the opening of the sitting today.
Under the Department of Justice Act, chapter 71 of our statutes, "The Minister of Justice shall have the superintendence of all matters connected with the administration of justice in Canada, not within the jurisdiction of the governments of the provinces." Under section 91 (21) of the British North America Act the federal government has exclusive legislative authority over bankruptcy matters. As the minister well knows, under this authority parliament has made the Minister of Justice responsible for the administration of the Bankruptcy Act. That is to be found in chapter 14 of our revised statutes. According to a government booklet entitled "The Organization of the Government of Canada":
The administration of the Bankruptcy Act is under the supervision of the Superintendent of Bankruptcy, whose duty it is to ensure the efficient carrying out of the provisions of the act, who has certain powers of control over the trustees throughout Canada in the discharge of their duties, and who generally investigates and reports to the Minister of Justice on matters pertaining to the administration of the act.
In particular, parliament has given the Minister of Justice the exclusive power to authorize, if he considers it will be of public advantage so to do, the issue of a licence to a person to act as a trustee. The minister is thus solely responsible for the conduct of a trustee while the trustee holds that licence or any renewal thereof. I do not think it can be argued for a moment that a trustee is not a federal official appointed under the provisions of the bankruptcy legislation.
To counterbalance the responsibility thus placed upon the minister, under section 3, parliament has given the superintendent power to make or cause to be made investigations outside his office, and when it appears a licensed trustee has been guilty of any improper conduct the superintendent may report and make recommendations to the minister. The superintendent may report that his powers of investigation are not enough. In such case he may recommend to the minister that the minister avail himself of the more extensive powers that parliament has given to the minister under part II of the Inquiries Act, chapter 154 of our statutes. Section 6 of that act provides:
The minister presiding over any department of the civil service of Canada may appoint at any time, under the authority of the governor in council, a commissioner or commissioners to investigate and

report upon the state and management of the business, or any part of the business, of such department, either in the inside or outside service thereof, and the conduct of any person in such service, so far as the same relates to his official duties.

These are the methods that have been approved by parliament and these are the powers given by parliament to the Minister of Justice as the methods to be employed by him and the powers to be exercised by him in investigating the administration and the conduct of the public business entrusted to him by parliament. These methods and powers are investigative and in some aspects inquisitorial beyond the processes of the common law. He also pointed out that the minister would have under him the administration of the anti-combines legislation.
The minister said that the purpose of this legislation was to provide competition which would be a spur to efficiency. What is the purpose, Mr. Chairman, of having efficiency in business organization if it is not to lower the price of the product and provide cheaper goods for the consumer? Surely the anti-combines legislation and the restrictive trade practices commission have been designed for years to act as instruments for the protection of the Canadian consuming public.
The minister also mentioned the patent law and the Trade Marks Act which primarily are designed to protect the consumer. He also made reference to bankruptcy. We in this party would prefer to see the bankruptcy and insolvency legislation under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Justice for the same reason that we argue that the R.C.M.P. should be under the direction of the Minister of Justice, namely, because the enforcement agencies that would implement the basic purposes of the bankruptcy legislation ought to be under the Minister of Justice. But even assuming that the bankruptcy and insolvency legislation are left with the proposed minister of consumer affairs, surely the purpose of bankruptcy and insolvency legislation is to protect the consumers. If there are losses owing to frauds in bankruptcy, ultimately the cost is passed on to the consumer.
The minister spoke of the Companies Act legislation for the supervision of the activities of companies. Again I point out that these companies exist specifically to serve the community and to sell to the consumer. Every piece of legislation which will come under the supervision of this new department ultimately has to do with the consumer. Therefore it is completely fallacious to argue that calling this department the department of consumer affairs will narrow its functions.
On the contrary, Mr. Chairman, we propose that its functions shall be widened. We cannot make this proposal under clause 6 but when clause 8 comes before the committee we shall propose that the clause be amended so as to give to the department and to the minister of consumer affairs powers with regard to two very important matters, one of which is to provide consumer protection.
The minister has already said that some 13 private bills are before the house dealing with consumer credit. Surely, Mr. Chairman, that underlines the tremendous interest and

Government Organization concern existing in Canada today with respect to the exploitation of the consumer which is now taking place on the part of small finance companies owing to the failure to disclose interest rates properly. Surely the time has come to set up a department to which the necessary powers will be granted to protect the public from small loans companies and loan sharks, to protect the housewife against misleading advertising and packaging and to guarantee the safety and quality of goods sold over the counter. If this department is going to serve the consumer, these are the kind of powers it will require.
Most important of all, Mr. Chairman, we think that such a department would have to have power to review consumer prices. This is something which the members of this party have been talking about now for at least a year and a half. We have drawn the attention of the government to the fact that the cost of living is spiralling at an accelerated rate.
The cost of living has gone up 4 per cent in the past 12 months and there is every indication that it will go up another 4 per cent in the coming 12 months. The Minister of Finance has himself budgeted on the basis that it will go up 3J per cent, but that does not tell the whole story. The 4 per cent increase during the past 12 months is over the whole range of consumer goods.
For example, if one takes the list of 20 or 30 commodities which the average family must buy in order to maintain a minimum standard of decency, then the increase is much more than 4 per cent. In comparing April, 1965 with April, 1966 I noticed that while on all consumer items the cost of living went up percentage points, on food the cost went up 10.3 percentage points.
Items like food, clothing and drugs are items which the average family must buy. There are other items which they can postpone buying or which they can forego, but things like food, clothing, drugs and the payment of rent must be budgeted for and the increase in these costs has been a great deal more than 4 per cent.

The tragedy is, Mr. Chairman, that the government refuses to be concerned about the rising cost of living. So what happens? There are two categories of persons who are affected. For them an increase in the cost of

The second group of persons are those receiving wages and salaries. The only way they can cope with the rising cost of living is to ask for more money. This is why we now have a rash of labour disputes from one end of Canada to the other. This is why the Minister of Labour is being harassed with the longshoremen's strike, with the dispute between Air Canada and its employees, with the dispute between the seaway employees and the seaway authority. In almost every province of Canada today strike votes are being taken and labour discord is rife, not because workers are anxious to go on strike-anyone who has that illusion ought to try walking the streets or manning a picket line week after week without any income to realize that going on strike is no picnic-but because they have no other recourse.
Unless workers can have more wages their standard of living must go down. Wages have lagged behind the rising cost of living and increased productivity. Workers in all parts of Canada are now asking for increased wages as they negotiate new collective bargaining agreements.
The government, which would not do anything about the rising cost of living, now finds labour disputes on its doorstep. You see, Mr. Chairman, in the period this government has been in office it has never faced its problems. It has thought that it could solve its problems by sweeping them under the rug. Anybody realizes that when you sweep problems under a rug they multiply. Instead of having one problem you end up with six. That is exactly what has happened to the government. It is faced with labour discord, strikes and threats of strikes which loom up all across Canada, because during its 18 months in office it has turned its blind eye to the problem of rising living costs.
I suppose, following the statement of the Minister of Labour on Friday, the government thinks that the answer lies in putting the cork into the neck of the bottle and stopping these requests for higher wages. The minister spoke the other day about the possibility of setting up labour courts. I think the government may as well know that the working people of Canada will never stand for any government allowing somebody to adjudicate the price of their labour while at the same time refusing to adjudicate on the prices the

monopolies and combines demand for the products they sell in the consumer market. You cannot have a free market for the large corporations and a fixed, determined market governing the price which people get for their labour.
That is why we want to see a department of consumers affairs established. That is why we want set up under such a department a prices review board that will examine prices. If there is justification for setting up conciliation boards and arbitration boards to determine whether an increase in wages is justified, surely there is a case for setting up a tribunal to determine whether an increase in prices is justified. That is all we have been asking.
If the government once more turns down this suggestion it need not be surprised if labour disputes continue, if more farmers, as in Quebec, wheel their tractors out on the highway declaring that they will not pay their taxes. The government need not be surprised if the farmers on the prairies, finding that wheat, the main commodity they have to sell, has gone down in price while their cost of production has gone up, cry out in protest.
That is why we feel that this amendment is more than merely changing the name of a department from department of the "registrar general" to the department of consumer affairs. This amendment asks the government to set aside one department which, in addition to the duties already outlined by the minister having to do with anti-combines legislation, bankruptcy, the Trade Marks Act and the Companies Act, all of which concern consumers directly or indirectly, shall be charged with the positive and definite responsibility of protecting the consuming public of Canada against exploitation, against deception and against selfish and greedy profiteering.

If the Minister of Finance is right in his prediction that the cost of living in the next 12 months, as it has done in the previous 12 months, will rise by 3i to 4 per cent, then

Before I commence my remarks on this subject I should like to say a word of encouragement to the new members of parliament in connection with any bills or notices of motion they may put on the order paper. time a number of sessions as well as an election have intervened and a new parliament is in progress.

This will mean that they will be able to air their views.
I suggest that the motion today is an interesting one, not just because it is in my name and seconded by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Davis) but because it does cover an area of increasing public concern. Regardless of the disposal of this motion today, Mr. Speaker, I hope we have a good discussion of it. There are three purposes underlying the notice of motion and I should like to put them forward for consideration. The first is that such representation on the boards of directors of crown corporations would serve as a taxpayers' watch dog. Second-I will elaborate on this as I go on-there is an opportunity provided for involvement and participation on the part of members of parliament. I believe that this involvement and participation is very much in line with the thinking of most of the private members of parliament these days is something which could be raised, and we should be working toward that end. This raising of the status of private members is the third purpose of the notice of motion.
With regard to the first point of having what I call a taxpayers' watch dog on various crown corporations, and they fall into different categories, this is doubly necessary at a time of increasing expenditure on the part of public bodies which largely are cut off from any direct responsibility to the taxpayers, the people who in some instances are subsidizing their very operation.
I might not have put this motion on the order paper if that trend toward indirect

spending had been diminishing rather than increasing, but there is an increasing trend toward what I consider to be a deflection away from the principle for which parliament was originally set up. Basically, I think the original and perhaps only purpose of parliament was to make a very close examination and give final approval or rejection of the spending of tax dollars. I have heard it said in this house that really this is the main purpose of the House of Commons, to pass estimates and approve the spending of tax dollars.
The matter which concerns me, Mr. Speaker, and I believe should concern every member of the house, is that increasing amounts of tax dollars are being put at the disposal of non-elected people and bodies whose only responsibility to the public, through this house, is to a minister of the crown. We all know the position of ministers of the crown who report to the house on behalf of crown corporations when questions are put to them. I suggest that the only reply they can make is that they will refer the questions to the crown corporations concerned and will report back to the house. The min ster really only serves as a channel to obtain the opinions of people serving on a non-elected board.
May I, Mr. Speaker, in case we do not realize the amount of money involved quickly run down some of the figures about which we are talking today. If I might digress a little, when this motion was placed on the order paper a little over two years ago considerable attention and publicity was given to it in the press, and some interest by way of correspondence was also shown.
I am not saying that the motion is perfect in all respects, but the idea of more direct control over spending by the House of Commons did seem to receive quite favourable comment and commendation in the press. At any rate, one article outlined the three types of agencies or corporations. There were three groups: the agency corporations, the proprietary corporations and other corporations.
In the first group appear such giants as Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, with a budget of $62 million. Then there were Crown Assets Disposal Corporation with a budget of $6.5 million, the National Capital Commission with an $84.4 million budget, the National Harbours Board with a $470.7 million budget, and Northern Canada Power Commission with a budget of $28.5 million.

The figures in the second category are as follows, and I presume that these figures are now two years out of date. There are such proprietary corporations as the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, with a budget of $108.3 million, the Canadian National Railways with assets of $3,754 million, Overseas Telecommunications, $61.8 million, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, $2,000 million, St. Lawrence Seaway Authority, $507.3 million and, of course, there is the Bank of Canada with assets of $3,300 million.
My point, Mr. Speaker, is that these are terrific sums of money which have been placed in the hands of corporations some of which operate at a profit. Of course, profit is a relative thing, so I do not think that is a great point; but some of them do operate under a deficit, and I think that is a very pertinent consideration. We have placed huge sums of money at the disposal of these corporations, some of which are subsidized with the taxpayers' money, but no direct control over them is exercised by members of parliament.
My understanding as a representative of a constituency is that one of my duties here is to keep track, as much a I can, of taxpayers' dollars and how and where they are being spent. Some people fear the political control which one member of parliament might exert over the board of directors of one of these crown corporations. However, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that this is a fallacious argument against this proposal. I cannot see that one member of parliament, even if he be most loquacious, in the minority position he would be in on a board of 15 or 20 directors would have a very disastrous effect on that board.

Quite frankly, Mr. Speaker, it is pretty galling to me when as a member of parliament I return to my riding to be blamed and criticized by taxpayers for some decision taken by a crown corporation over which I or this parliament have no control and no opportunity at the policy-making level at least to present a point of view. My next point has to do with raising the status of members of parliament. There has been a move in the last few years around here, not just by public relations and press releases but by making possible new areas of opportunity, to raise the status of the member of parliament and to attempt to employ more of his experience. We have a tremendous amount of experience in this house springing from the municipal level, the legal and engineering fields and other fields. There has been quite a move to try to raise the status of members of parliament. I suggest one of the best ways this can be done is for a member of parliament to have an opportunity, on behalf of parliament and the taxpayers, of becoming involved at the director's level in the operation of some of our crown corporations. I do not see any objection to this sort of thing.
One of the problems that the backbencher or member of parliament has to face is that he has to try to cover a whole field of knowledge and try to know a little about everything. My own view is that a parliamentarian could carve out a career for himself by becoming expert in one or two fields, thus being of great assistance to this house. If we
Crown Corporations
had hon. members from any side of the house who in debate could give us facts that we do not always get now, it would be to the benefit of this house. Sometimes when a minister has to report to the house he is only reporting information that in my judgment could be called hearsay, although such report is often written and comes from a crown corporation.
May I mention another thing that may not be generally known. Many crown corporations do not come under the control of the Auditor General. I understand that many crown corporations, especially the ones running at a deficit, do not use the services or come under the aegis of the Auditor General. The Auditor General of Canada does not have the same authority with respect to crown corporations in the examining of their books as he has with government departments. In that regard the crown corporations are doubly cut off, so to speak, from public scrutiny in the expenditure of money.
Some other countries do not employ the techniques I have suggested and I am sure that other speakers will mention this fact. I can only tell hon. members of one country where they go much farther in these matters than my suggestion. Members of the two chambers of the Swedish parliament are elected by parliament as members of the boards of directors of two institutions in Sweden which are placed directly under parliamentary control, namely, the Bank of Sweden and the National Debt Office. The members of parliament are elected for a period of three years. They represent all the democratic political parties represented in the Riksdag and are members of considerable experience in parliamentary life. Members of parliament are appointed by the government to the boards of directors of more important government-owned corporations in Sweden as, for instance, the Ore Mining Company of Kiruna, the Tobacco Monopoly, the Kredit-banken which is the state bank for commercial transactions, the Scandinavian Airlines System, and the like. Members of parliament are also elected by the government to the boards of directors of privately-owned insurance companies in Sweden. I do not suggest that we in this country go as far as this.
I believe that a careful reading of my resolution will allay any fears on the part of those people who think that what I propose would go this far. I suggest that my resolution would return to the members of this parliament one of the basic rights and basic responsibilities that we have, which is the

Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to enter this debate until I first considered who was moving the motion. However, after listening to the very interesting comments of the hon. member who has just spoken I think I should say a word or two. At the outset I cannot think of any reason why this matter could not be referred to the committee that the hon. member suggests. There would be greater opportunity for considering his proposal in committee because our time is limited here.
I throw out just a few ideas with regard to the motion. It is attractive at first glance. How practical it is is something that would have to be considered.
I think the hon. member is quite right when he says that the main function of parliament, which still subsists, is to determine how much money shall be exacted from the people by taxation and then to scrutinize very carefully how that money shall be spent. Although that purpose still lies with parliament and although we try to exercise it, we all know it is very difficult to maintain that

supervision over taxation and expenditure that we should like. On the other hand, I do not think it is quite right to suggest that many of these crown corporations are not subjected to rather careful scrutiny. I had a fair bit of experience with this in days gone by, particularly with Atomic Energy of Canada Limited for which I reported to this house for about six years.
[DOT] (6:30 p.m.)
Atomic Energy of Canada Limited is not a profit-making organization; it is one of those in which we invest money year after year. We have done so regularly with general approval, as well as with great success judging by the results that have been achieved. My point in this connection is that as the minister responsible for this corporation I was obliged, after meeting with the directors and hearing their views as to their requirements, to put their suggestions before treasury board and before the cabinet. So an examination of the expenditure contemplated by the organization was carried out by channels competent to consider the matter.
Treasury board, which is a committee of ministers of the crown assisted by officials, is very well qualified to examine requests for money. From my own experience, sometimes treasury board can be ruthless in rejecting even the soundest arguments for utilizing tax money in certain directions. My recollection is that a careful examination of requirements was made by treasury board and by cabinet before the government consented to present to parliament a request for an allocation of money to be made to Atomic Energy of Canada.
I believe this applies to all the crown corporations the hon. member mentioned. So although members of parliament are not sitting on the boards of these corporations numerous members of parliament, particularly those in the cabinet, are directly concerned. They, treasury board and finally the whole cabinet have a chance to look carefully at the proposed expenditure. In this way there is a review of expenditure.
On the other hand, it is true that parliament as a whole does not have the same opportunity for detailed study as is given to members of the cabinet. Whether or not the hon. member's suggestion would result in an improvement, I do not know. If members of parliament were appointed to these boards it would certainly provide opportunities for them to become more or less expert in the operation of some of these organizations. This
May 30, 1966

would obviously be an advantage. However, at the moment I do not consider that parliament as a whole would gain appreciably. One or two members might learn a lot about the operation of Atomic Energy of Canada or Polymer or C.N.R. or the National Capital Commission but I am not sure whether their contribution in the house would be greater than that made by those members of the cabinet who have responsibility for these organizations. And we all know that opportunity to discuss such matters, whether in committee or not, is limited.
I ask the hon. member this question. How does one guard against the involvement of a member of parliament sitting on a board of directors which is spending money and letting contracts in respect of which decisions have to be made by the board? Would the member of parliament have a vote in connection, say, with the letting of substantial contracts to some firm? And if he were involved to such an extent, would this be wise? Suppose some difficulty arose in a corporation- fortunately, we have been free from this and I hope we shall continue to be free from it-because of a mistake being made or because funds were misappropriated. If, following some quite innocent action or ignorance or inertia on his part, something went wrong with the affairs of the corporation, he might be very much embarrassed. I put this forward for the hon. member's consideration.

never bothered me when I first came to this house and sat against the curtains at the back, a position in the house which I found much more agreeable than any other place I have occupied because you are not under the same amount of observation and you can ease yourself out of the chamber without being noticed, whereas when you get to the first or second rows it is noticeable when you rise and leave.
I have never been bothered by this question of the status of a member of parliament. When I was a backbencher it did not bother me. I do not know why it should bother anybody. As all of us here know that it is a considerable achievement to get elected. A member who makes himself an expert in any field generally gets the ear of the House of Commons. In my experience it is up to the individual member to do the work, get the information and acquire the knowledge so that he is listened to by his colleagues in the house.
I am not at all certain that raising the status of a member of the house is one of the factors that should be considered in this otherwise interesting proposition. Status rests with the member himself. When a matter comes up in the house upon which a member is recognized as somewhat of an expert he is immediately called upon to represent his party and participate in the debate.
